questions.q: Which three layers does this lesson say every governance architecture has to provide?
options: Metadata and catalog, policy and enforcement, and integration
Marketing, sales, and finance
Frontend, backend, and database only
Hiring, training, and performance review
questions.explain: The lesson names three required layers: metadata/catalog, policy/enforcement, and integration.

questions.q: Which reference-architecture pattern does centralized governance pair with, per this lesson?
options: Hub-and-spoke
Mesh of catalogs
Catalog-of-catalogs
No shared pattern at all
questions.explain: Centralized governance pairs with hub-and-spoke: one team, one central hub, every platform feeding in.

questions.q: In the hub-and-spoke pattern, how does metadata flow?
options: Every platform feeds metadata into a single central hub
Each platform only shares metadata directly with one other platform
Metadata never leaves its originating platform
There is no catalog of any kind in this pattern
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke centralizes metadata collection: every platform (spoke) feeds into one central hub.

questions.q: What are the four parts of the standard architecture-principle template used in this lesson?
options: Name, statement, rationale, implications
Title, author, date, version
Budget, timeline, owner, status
Problem, solution, cost, benefit
questions.explain: The lesson's template has four parts: name, statement, rationale, and implications.

questions.q: In the worked insurance-company example, which model do the five factors point toward?
options: A federated rollout scoped specifically to claims and underwriting, with marketing staying separately governed
A full, unscoped data-mesh rollout across all three domains immediately
A fully centralized model covering all three domains with one hub
No governance architecture at all, since insurance data doesn't need it
questions.explain: Given cross-cutting regulated data in claims/underwriting but independent marketing data, limited platform budget, and existing capability gaps, the factors point to a narrowly scoped federated model.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what distinguishes a 'data product' from a plain raw table?
options: It meets characteristics like discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, and secure — it has real consumers it's built for
It is always stored in exactly one specific database technology
It must be owned by the central IT department
It has no schema of any kind
questions.explain: The lesson lists six characteristics a data product has to meet, which a plain raw table doesn't automatically satisfy.

questions.q: What are the three architectural components centralized governance needs, per this lesson?
options: A single enterprise metadata hub, a single policy engine, and a single access-provisioning queue
Multiple independent catalogs with no coordination
A central index plus fully autonomous domain catalogs
No metadata layer is needed at all
questions.explain: The lesson names three required components: one metadata hub, one policy engine, one access-provisioning queue.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is decentralized governance a fourth reference-architecture pattern alongside hub-and-spoke and catalog-of-catalogs?
options: No — it's the absence of a shared architecture pattern, not a pattern itself
Yes, it is architecturally identical to hub-and-spoke
Yes, it is a stricter version of catalog-of-catalogs
Yes, it always includes a central index by definition
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states decentralized is not a fourth legitimate pattern — it's defined by the absence of a shared metadata layer.

questions.q: What happens to a catalog's usefulness if its harvesting layer is incomplete, even with a polished UI?
options: The catalog remains incomplete — the UI can't fix what the harvesting layer never captured
The UI automatically fills in any missing metadata
It has no effect, because the UI is the only part that matters
The catalog becomes a data dictionary instead
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a catalog is only as complete as what its underlying harvesting/storage architecture actually captured.

questions.q: In classification-driven masking, what role does the sensitivity tag play?
options: It actively drives real-time enforcement — a masking policy attached to the tag applies automatically on every future query
It is purely decorative and has no effect on query results
It only appears in a quarterly compliance report
It requires a human to manually approve every single query before masking applies
questions.explain: The tag isn't just a catalog label — it's the mechanism that triggers the masking policy automatically, with no human in that loop.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe lineage as fundamentally a graph-traversal problem?
options: Real lineage questions, like tracing everything downstream of a column, require following multiple hops across assets and transformations
Graphs are required by data privacy regulations
Lineage can only ever be stored in a graph database, with no alternative
Table-level lineage eliminates the need for any traversal at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains that answering real lineage questions means traversing several hops across a directed graph, not a single lookup.

questions.q: In a federated metadata architecture, how is metadata typically organized?
options: Multiple stores, often per domain or platform, connected by APIs that sync or query across them
One single store that every team is required to use
No storage at all — metadata is regenerated on every query
A single spreadsheet shared across the whole organization
questions.explain: Federated architecture spreads metadata across multiple stores rather than one central repository, connected by integration rather than consolidation.

questions.q: What is the main architectural drawback of RBAC as fine-grained distinctions multiply?
options: Roles multiply quickly, since every new fine distinction needs its own role
RBAC cannot be audited at all
RBAC requires attribute evaluation at request time
RBAC only works with unstructured data
questions.explain: The lesson gives the example of "analysts who can see EU but not US customers" becoming its own role — RBAC scales roles, not rules.

questions.q: Why does a permission mistake in Microsoft Fabric tend to be tenant-wide by default?
options: Because every Fabric workload — lakehouse, warehouse, BI, pipelines — stores its data in one shared tenant-wide lake, OneLake
Because Fabric has no access control features at all
Because Fabric only supports a single user per tenant
Because Fabric workloads each use entirely separate, disconnected storage
questions.explain: Fabric's own governance course is explicit that the shared OneLake architecture — not separate storage per workload — is why mistakes have tenant-wide reach by default.

questions.q: Why does expressing governance rules as code enable CI/CD-style discipline?
options: Because a text file can go through pull-request review, automated testing, and version-control rollback, the same way application code already does
Because code files are always smaller than console settings
Because CI/CD pipelines cannot run any kind of test on configuration settings
Because policy as code eliminates the need for any review process
questions.explain: The lesson's central CI/CD argument is that a versioned file can be reviewed, tested, and rolled back exactly like application code.

questions.q: What does a scheduled compliance scan catch that a CI/CD pipeline check would not?
options: Policy drift — a manual change made to an already-deployed resource, outside any pipeline
Syntax errors in the policy file itself
Network latency issues
Changes that are still in a pull request and haven't merged yet
questions.explain: A CI/CD check only fires on proposed changes going through the pipeline; a scheduled scan catches changes made directly to already-deployed resources.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an undocumented governance architecture becomes 'folklore'?
options: Because the reasons behind decisions get forgotten once the people who made them leave or move on
Because folklore is a required deliverable in enterprise architecture
Because diagrams are not allowed to be stored digitally
Because architecture only matters during the kickoff meeting
questions.explain: Without documentation, a new architect or board member can't recover why a decision was made — only the decision survives, not the reasoning.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a roadmap add on top of a governance strategy?
options: A time-ordered sequence of the strategy's priorities that people can plan and budget against
A replacement business case that ignores the original strategy
A single fixed deadline for the entire program
A list of software vendors to purchase immediately
questions.explain: The strategy supplies the why and what; the roadmap supplies the when and in what order — a real sequence, not just a list.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as a common way governance strategies fail?
options: Trying to govern every domain and platform at once instead of sequencing priorities
Focusing on too few initiatives in the first year
Having too many named executive sponsors
Documenting the maturity assessment too thoroughly
questions.explain: Attempting centralized governance over everything simultaneously stalls — most organizations need to sequence and choose where to start.

questions.q: What is an architecture decision record (ADR), according to this lesson?
options: A short, dated document capturing one specific decision — context, decision, and consequences
A live dashboard tracking every open governance ticket
A legal contract between two business units
A quarterly budget spreadsheet
questions.explain: An ADR is a short, historical record of one specific decision, written once and rarely edited afterward.

questions.q: Per the lesson, what distinguishes a complete design package from an incomplete one?
options: Every step has a specific answer tied to the chosen scenario, not a restatement of generic course definitions
It must be at least twenty pages long
It must include a professionally designed slide deck
It must name a real company by name
questions.explain: The lesson's self-review instruction is explicit: check for genuine specificity tied to the scenario, not generic restated definitions.

questions.q: Why did the compliance/risk officer get a standing seat on Northbridge's review board instead of a rotating one?
options: Regulatory risk decisions can't wait for a rotation schedule
No other roles were available to serve on the board
The board was required by law to have exactly one member
Rotating seats are prohibited in financial services governance
questions.explain: The lesson notes that, unlike Castellan's rotating domain reps, Northbridge gave compliance a standing seat because of the stakes involved.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most common reason a technically sound governance architecture design fails to get support?
options: A presentation that leads with the architecture diagram instead of the problem it solves
The architecture was designed using the wrong color scheme
Executives never attend any governance meetings
ADRs are not allowed to be shown to any audience
questions.explain: The lesson states the most common failure isn't the design itself — it's presenting it in a way that leads with architecture instead of the problem.

questions.q: Why did the platform decision in Chapter 4 get written up as its own ADR?
options: It was an expensive, hard-to-reverse choice that needed a recorded reason
ADRs are required for every minor software setting
The board requested a PowerPoint instead
ADRs are only used for security incidents
questions.explain: Choosing one enterprise catalog over standardizing on a single ERP vendor's tools was exactly the kind of significant, hard-to-reverse decision Lesson 25 says deserves an ADR.
